segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter Ames kept his shop two streets above the place where the Hartsford hill gave out and the water began. It smelled of bay and dust and something sharp underneath. He swept a row of herb bundles off the counter to make room for four pairs of elbows, and he listened while Jory Brennick told it in order: the long back room, the bench of cracked glass, the stone mortar the size of a wash basin, the strongbox bolted at chest height to an oak post.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: That's no cellar. Nobody grinds in their cellar with a mortar you'd need two men to lift.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: No. No, they don't.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: And the wall by the post's been chiselled. Five bites out of it, square-edged, grey as a fresh break. Everything else down there has twenty years of weed on it. Those have nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter's hand had gone up to the loupe at his throat without his noticing it.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: The lock has no keyhole. There's letters standing proud off the plate, spaced like a name. And it was warm, Mr Ames. Warm through a wet glove, in water that aches your jaw.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter went into the back and came out with the oilcloth. He unfolded the letter on the counter and turned past the first page, which he had plainly read a hundred times, to the second, which he had not.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: She writes about the fishers bringing things up off the bottom that autumn. There was a crack opened in the seabed when the land went down, and pieces of it came up in the nets. She calls it the stone that bleeds light.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: They still come up.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: She ground it. That's what the mortar's for. There was a fever in the camps that first winter, up where people were putting roofs on the hill, and she lost a good many of them and could do nothing. So she tried what nobody had tried. She says here she wrote down every measure, and burned the first three sets of measures as useless.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: And the fourth?

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: The fourth she kept.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He read on with his finger under the line, and his voice got slower rather than quieter.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: She sealed her notes and a sample of the stone in the box, and she made the lock out of the same stone. She says it answers to the household's true name, spoken three times, in open air. Never under the water. She is firm about that twice over.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Then the box has to come up before anyone says a word.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: There's more. She writes, it will have its price of whoever speaks. I could not learn the price beforehand, and I would not ask another to pay it in my place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nobody said anything to that for a moment. Maud Brennick folded her arms and looked at the shelf of jars behind Walter's head.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: That's an honest sentence. I'd rather it weren't.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The shop bell went. Selah Vance ducked under the lintel with her coat still dripping from the walk up and her cap in her hand.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: They told me at the landing you'd all come up here. I came to hear whether you'd got into it.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: We're in. Through a gap in the wall the tremor opened. There's cut marks beside it, fresh ones, and none of us can account for them.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: I can. That'll be my survey crew. Two of them went down last week with a bar to set marks for the piling line, and the wall there is the only stone standing straight enough to cut into. Three days before the quarter moon. I've got it in the book if you want to see it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora Quill let out a breath and started laughing, and stopped herself.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: That's the good half of what I came to say. The weather past the point has turned faster than the harbour men called it. I can't drive in a sea and I'll not have the frame out there when it hits.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She put her cap back on.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: Pilings go in four days. Not six.
